questions.enonce_markdown:
The term Logic is derived from the Greek word "Logos" which means?

*Options as printed:* A) Organon.   B) Discourse.   C) Thinking.   D) Reasoning.
themes: O Level Logic - nature and scope of logic
questions.corrige_markdown:
"Logos" is a Greek word with several accepted meanings: word, discourse, thought and reason. Three of the four printed options (Discourse, Thinking, Reasoning) are all given in standard textbooks as the meaning of "logos", so the question cannot be marked reliably. "Organon" is wrong: it is the title Aristotle's logical works received later, not the root of the word.

**Intended answer: "Logos" means word, discourse, thought or reason (Organon is the only wrong option).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically, so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The most appropriate reason why the study of Logic is important is that it enables one to:

*Options as printed:* A) Gain clarity and precision in speech.   B) Perceive the coherence and incoherence of terms.   C) Investigate and detect true argument.   D) Weigh the pros and cons of propositions.
themes: O Level Logic - nature and scope of logic
questions.corrige_markdown:
Logic is important because it gives standards for telling good reasoning from bad reasoning, which includes seeing whether an argument is valid and weighing the reasons for and against a claim. Option A (clarity of speech) is a by-product, B speaks of "terms" when coherence concerns propositions and arguments, C wrongly speaks of a "true" argument (arguments are valid or invalid, not true or false), and D is defensible. The printed key cannot be fixed with certainty, so the question is left open.

**Intended answer: Logic enables us to distinguish valid from invalid reasoning and to weigh reasons for and against a claim (D is the closest option).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically, so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: "A form five boy was caught cheating in an exam, and it was later concluded that all form five boys are exam cheats". This is an example of:
themes: O Level Logic - nature and scope of logic
questions.corrige_markdown:
The conclusion about ALL form five boys is drawn from one observed case. Reasoning from particular cases to a general statement is induction (here a hasty generalisation). It is not deductive, because the conclusion goes beyond what the premise guarantees, and it is not analogical, because no comparison between two things is made. "Logical reasoning" is too general to be a type.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following Laws of Thought is expressed in the formula A=A?
themes: O Level Logic - laws of thought
questions.corrige_markdown:
The formula $A = A$ says that a thing is the same as itself: this is the Principle (Law) of Identity. Excluded Middle is $A \vee \sim A$, and Contradiction (non-contradiction) is $\sim(A \cdot \sim A)$.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The Operation of the Mind in which ideas are compared is known as:
themes: O Level Logic - nature and scope of logic
questions.corrige_markdown:
The three operations of the mind are simple apprehension (forming ideas), judgment (comparing two ideas and affirming or denying one of the other) and reasoning (passing from judgments to a new judgment). Comparing ideas is judging. Reasoning compares judgments, and abstraction forms ideas.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Identify the fields that both deal with thinking:
themes: O Level Logic - nature and scope of logic
questions.corrige_markdown:
Psychology studies how people actually think (the mental process), while Logic studies how people ought to think correctly (the standards of valid reasoning). Both therefore deal with thinking. History, Law and Science use reasoning but do not take thinking itself as their subject.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The terms "Teacher and Learner" are adequately known as:
themes: O Level Logic - terms and their classification
questions.corrige_markdown:
Correlative terms are terms that imply each other: there is no teacher without a learner and no learner without a teacher (like husband and wife, parent and child). Contrary terms are extremes of one scale (hot and cold) and contradictory terms exclude each other with nothing in between (guilty and not guilty).

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Two Terms in which one negates the other are considered as:
themes: O Level Logic - terms and their classification
questions.corrige_markdown:
Contradictory terms are a term and its negation (healthy and non-healthy): they cannot both apply to the same thing and they cannot both be denied of it. Contrary terms (black and white) cannot both apply but both can be denied (grey), so one does not simply negate the other.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The statement of an essential attribute of terms is known as:
themes: O Level Logic - terms and their classification
questions.corrige_markdown:
The connotation (intension) of a term is the set of essential attributes that a thing must have to be called by that term. Denotation (extension) is the set of things to which the term applies.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The Function of language to cause or prevent action is:
themes: O Level Logic - nature and scope of logic
questions.corrige_markdown:
The function of language that aims to cause or prevent action (commands, requests, instructions) is the directive function. The printed word "Directory" is a misprint of "Directive" and is the only option that matches. Informative and cognitive language conveys information, and expressive language shows feelings.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which Language Function is expressed in the sentence, "Oh what a wonderful party!"?
themes: O Level Logic - nature and scope of logic
questions.corrige_markdown:
The sentence expresses the speaker's feelings. This is the emotive (expressive) function of language. It gives no information to be tested and issues no command.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Identify from below that which is False of the relation between Language and Thought:
themes: O Level Logic - nature and scope of logic
questions.corrige_markdown:
Language is the vehicle of thought: it permits us to express ideas, expresses thoughts and can place ideas in a context. It does not dominate thought, because thought comes first and language serves it. Option C is therefore the false statement.

**Answer: C.**

choix.texte: Language permits one to express ideas.

questions.enonce_markdown: A word or words used in explaining a term is/are known as:
themes: O Level Logic - definition and division
questions.corrige_markdown:
In a definition, the term to be defined is the definiendum and the word or words that explain it are the definiens. Only D matches "words used in explaining a term".

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A kind of Definition which gives meaning to a brand new term is:
themes: O Level Logic - definition and division
questions.corrige_markdown:
A stipulative definition assigns a meaning to a new term (or a new meaning to an old one), as when a scientist names a new discovery. A lexical definition reports the existing dictionary use of a word.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The expression, "Logic is everywhere, even in the air we breathe" most adequately represents:
themes: O Level Logic - definition and division
questions.corrige_markdown:
The sentence uses emotionally loaded, rhetorical language to make us feel that logic matters, rather than to state the exact meaning of the word. A definition meant to influence attitudes in this way is a persuasive definition.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which Fallacy is committed when a Definition is stated in Figurative language?
themes: O Level Logic - definition and division
questions.corrige_markdown:
A good definition must be clear. A definition in figurative, vague or ambiguous language ("Man is the glory of creation") hides the meaning instead of showing it: this is the fault of obscurity, the obscure definition. A circular definition uses the term in its own definiens.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: In Logical Division the Species into which the Genus is subdivided is adequately called:
themes: O Level Logic - definition and division
questions.corrige_markdown:
A logical division has three parts: the totum divisum (the whole or genus divided), the fundamentum divisionis (the basis of the division) and the membra dividentia (the dividing members, i.e. the species). The species are the membra dividentia.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
An assertion which is capable of being True or False is known as a:

*Options as printed:* A) Statement.   B) Proposition.   C) Sentence.   D) Phrase.
themes: O Level Logic - propositions and their types
questions.corrige_markdown:
An assertion that is either true or false is called a proposition in traditional logic and a statement in modern logic; the two words are used for the same thing in many textbooks. A sentence can be a question or a command and a phrase asserts nothing. Because both A and B are defensible, the question cannot be marked reliably.

**Intended answer: a proposition (also called a statement).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically, so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: A Proposition which is a straight forward affirmative or negative statement without a condition is best described as:
themes: O Level Logic - propositions and their types
questions.corrige_markdown:
A categorical proposition asserts or denies something unconditionally ("All men are mortal"). A hypothetical proposition has an "if ... then" condition, a disjunctive one an "either ... or", and a modal one states a mode (possible, necessary).

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A Proposition which asserts that "the members of one class are totally or partially excluded from another class", is most appropriately known as:
themes: O Level Logic - propositions and their types
questions.corrige_markdown:
Exclusion of one class from another, totally (E: No S is P) or partially (O: Some S is not P), is what a negative proposition does. An affirmative proposition includes a class in another, and universal and particular describe quantity, not quality.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The statement "Teachers are Intelligent Persons" can be translated into its optimum logical form as:
themes: O Level Logic - propositions and their types
questions.corrige_markdown:
An unquantified subject with an affirmative predicate is normally read as universal: "Teachers are intelligent persons" becomes the A proposition "All teachers are intelligent persons" (All S are P). Option D reverses subject and predicate, and A and B weaken the claim to particular propositions.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Identify the vowel corresponding to the Proposition whose Predicate Term is distributed and Subject Term is undistributed:
themes: O Level Logic - propositions and their types
questions.corrige_markdown:
Distribution: A distributes only the subject, E both terms, I neither, and O only the predicate. The proposition with an undistributed subject and a distributed predicate is O ("Some S are not P").

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which portion is shaded in representing the "A" Proposition on the Venn diagram?
themes: immediate inference and oppositions
questions.corrige_markdown:
The A proposition "All S are P" says that nothing is S and not P, so the part of S lying outside P is shaded as empty. That region is $S\bar{P}$. $SP$ is the overlap (shaded for the E proposition), and $\bar{S}P$ is the part of P outside S.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following is true of Immediate Inference?
themes: immediate inference and oppositions
questions.corrige_markdown:
Immediate inference draws a conclusion from a single proposition, with no middle term or second premise. A, C and D describe mediate inference (the syllogism), so they are false. The only option that can be true is B: the single proposition from which the process starts contains two terms, its subject and its predicate.

**Answer: B.**

choix.texte: The conclusion follows from two premises.
The process begins from two terms.
The conclusion follows from the three terms.

questions.enonce_markdown: Identify the pair which is made up of Forms of Opposition:
themes: immediate inference and oppositions
questions.corrige_markdown:
The forms of opposition are contradiction, contrariety, subcontrariety and subalternation. Obversion, contraposition, conversion and inversion are forms of eduction, not of opposition. Only B has two real forms of opposition.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The relationship between a Universal Affirmative Proposition and a Universal Negative Proposition in Opposition is called:
themes: immediate inference and oppositions
questions.corrige_markdown:
A (All S are P) and E (No S is P) are contraries: they cannot both be true, but they can both be false. Contradictories are A-O and E-I, subcontraries are I-O, and subalterns are A-I and E-O.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following Standard Form Categorical Propositions is not convertible in Eduction?
themes: immediate inference and oppositions
questions.corrige_markdown:
Conversion exchanges subject and predicate. E and I convert simply, and A converts by limitation into I (All S are P gives Some P are S). The O proposition cannot be converted at all, because after exchange the new subject would be distributed in the conclusion but was not in the premise (illicit process). So the particular negative is the one that is not convertible.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The most appropriate usefulness of the Syllogism is that it:

*Options as printed:* A) Helps in promoting hasty inference.   B) Is a test of inconsistency.   C) Promotes precise Arguments.   D) Is a vital tool for clarity in reasoning.
themes: categorical syllogisms and their rules
questions.corrige_markdown:
The syllogism is useful because it makes the structure of an argument explicit and lets us test its validity. A (hasty inference) is wrong, and B (inconsistency) is not its main use. C (precise arguments) and D (clarity in reasoning) both say the same thing in different words, so the question has two defensible answers and cannot be marked reliably.

**Intended answer: it promotes precise argument and clarity in reasoning (C or D).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically, so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
In a Categorical Syllogism, the Minor term helps to identify the:

*Options as printed:* A) Major premise.   B) Minor premise.   C) Conclusion.   D) Premises.
themes: categorical syllogisms and their rules
questions.corrige_markdown:
The minor term is the subject of the conclusion and it also appears in the minor premise, so it helps to identify the minor premise (the premise that contains it) and also the conclusion. Both B and C are defensible, so the question cannot be marked reliably. A is wrong: the major term identifies the major premise.

**Intended answer: the minor premise (B), although the conclusion (C) can also be argued.**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically, so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: Which Fallacy is committed in a Syllogistic Argument when a Conclusion is drawn from two Negative Premises?
themes: logical fallacies in arguments
questions.corrige_markdown:
One rule of the valid syllogism says that no conclusion follows from two negative premises. Breaking it is the fallacy of exclusive premises. Illicit major and illicit minor concern a term distributed in the conclusion but not in its premise, and undistributed middle concerns the middle term.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Determine the Figure of the following Syllogistic Argument: "All fruits are eatable thing. All oranges are fruits. Therefore, all oranges are eatable things"
themes: categorical syllogisms and their rules
questions.corrige_markdown:
Major term P = eatable things, minor term S = oranges, middle term M = fruits. The major premise is "All M are P" (M-P) and the minor premise is "All S are M" (S-M). The middle term is the subject of the major premise and the predicate of the minor premise: this is the First Figure (mood AAA, Barbara).

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: What is the most adequate Mood of this syllogism below? "No M are P. Some S are M. Therefore, some S are not P"
themes: categorical syllogisms and their rules
questions.corrige_markdown:
The mood is the sequence of the types of the major premise, the minor premise and the conclusion. "No M are P" is E, "Some S are M" is I, and "Some S are not P" is O. The mood is EIO (first figure, Ferio), a valid form. A check over all set models confirms that the conclusion cannot fail when both premises hold.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
All of the following Except ONE are requirements for putting Syllogisms into Valid Standard Form:

*Options as printed:* A) Determine the Premise Indicator.   B) Express the Syllogism into Standard Form.   C) Determine the Conclusion Indicator.   D) Respect the Structure of Syllogism.
themes: categorical syllogisms and their rules
questions.corrige_markdown:
To put an argument in standard form we find the conclusion (using conclusion indicators such as "therefore"), find the premises (using premise indicators such as "because"), name the major, minor and middle terms, and arrange the major premise, minor premise and conclusion in order while respecting the structure of the syllogism. The printed options mix the steps with the goal itself ("express into standard form" is the aim, not a step), so which one is the "exception" is not determined.

**Intended answer: not determined by the printed options; the steps are identifying the conclusion and premises and respecting the structure of the syllogism.**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically, so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
In diagramming Categorical Syllogisms, the First circle represents:

*Options as printed:* A) Predicate Term.   B) Middle Term.   C) Major Term.   D) Minor Term.
themes: categorical syllogisms and their rules
questions.corrige_markdown:
In a three-circle Venn diagram of a syllogism the circles stand for the minor, major and middle terms, but books differ on which circle is drawn first (the minor term in some, the major term in others), and "Predicate Term" is not a standard name for one of them. The key cannot be settled from the printed paper.

**Intended answer: not determined; the circles represent the minor, major and middle terms, in an order that depends on the textbook.**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically, so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: Which part of the Syllogism is omitted in the First order Enthymeme?
themes: categorical syllogisms and their rules
questions.corrige_markdown:
An enthymeme is a syllogism with one part left unstated. By the usual classification, the first-order enthymeme omits the major premise, the second-order omits the minor premise and the third-order omits the conclusion.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The Syllogism which furnishes the Conclusion for the next Syllogism is known as:
themes: categorical syllogisms and their rules
questions.corrige_markdown:
In a chain of syllogisms (a polysyllogism), the syllogism whose conclusion becomes a premise of the next one is the prosyllogism, and the syllogism that receives that conclusion as a premise is the episyllogism. The printed "Prosyllgism" is a misspelling of prosyllogism.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following applies to a Valid Mixed Hypothetical Syllogism (Modus Ponens)?
themes: conditional arguments and validity forms
questions.corrige_markdown:
In modus ponens the major premise is "If p then q", the minor premise affirms the antecedent ($p$) and the conclusion affirms the consequent ($q$). Denying the antecedent (A) and affirming the consequent (D) are the two classic fallacies, and B is wrong because the antecedent is affirmed in the minor premise, not in the conclusion.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Identify the pair below which constitute the types of Disjunctive Syllogism:
themes: dilemmas and disjunctive arguments
questions.corrige_markdown:
The two types of disjunctive syllogism are modus ponendo tollens (affirming one alternative denies the other, for an exclusive disjunction) and modus tollendo ponens (denying one alternative affirms the other). Modus ponens and modus tollens belong to the hypothetical (conditional) syllogism, and option A repeats the same name twice.

**Answer: D.**

choix.texte: Modus Tollendo Ponens and Modus Tollendo Ponens.
Modus Tollens and Modus Tollendo Ponens.
Modus Ponendo Tollens and Modus Ponens.
Modus Ponendo Tollens and Modus Tollendo Ponens.

questions.enonce_markdown: Determine the Form of the following Dilemma: "If the baby is sick, then he will be admitted in hospital and treated. The baby is neither admitted in hospital nor treated. Therefore, he is not sick"
themes: dilemmas and disjunctive arguments
questions.corrige_markdown:
The argument has one antecedent ("the baby is sick") and its consequences (admitted, treated) are denied, concluding that the antecedent is false. Denying the consequents to deny the antecedent is the destructive form, and a single antecedent makes it simple: a simple destructive form (modus tollens). A complex form would have two different antecedents and two different consequents.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Select the importance of the study of Fallacies:
themes: logical fallacies in arguments
questions.corrige_markdown:
Studying fallacies trains us to recognise and avoid errors in reasoning. B and D describe misusing arguments, and C is about judgment in general rather than reasoning errors.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following pair is made up of Informal Fallacies?
themes: logical fallacies in arguments
questions.corrige_markdown:
Informal fallacies come from the content or language of the argument. Petitio principii (begging the question) and accent (shifting the stress to change the meaning) are both informal fallacies. Undistributed middle and illicit process are formal (structural) fallacies of the syllogism, and obscure definition is a fault of definition, not an informal fallacy of argument.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: "Don't punish this child because he is an IDP", this reasoning commits the Fallacy of:
themes: logical fallacies in arguments
questions.corrige_markdown:
The speaker asks for pity for the child's situation (an internally displaced person) instead of giving a reason about what he did. Appeal to pity is the fallacy ad misericordiam. Ad hominem attacks the person, ad baculum threatens force and ad populum appeals to the crowd.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Identify that which best distinguishes the Fallacy of Converse Accident from the Fallacy of Accident:
themes: logical fallacies in arguments
questions.corrige_markdown:
Accident applies a general rule to a particular case it was not meant for (general to particular). Converse accident (hasty generalisation) draws a general rule from a few particular cases (particular to general). Here "the former" is converse accident and "the latter" is accident, so A is the correct contrast. Option B has them the wrong way round, because it describes accident as the former. C and D do not describe either fallacy.

**Answer: A.**

choix.texte: In the latter one moves quickly from generalization to particular case while in the former one moves quickly from particular case to generalization.
In the former one moves too quickly from the particular to general case while in the latter one moves too quickly from general case to particular case.
In the former one hastily draws a conclusion while in the latter one investigates.
In the latter a conclusion is drawn from facts while in the former the conclusion is not drawn from facts.

questions.enonce_markdown: The Fallacy of Composition is committed when:
themes: logical fallacies in arguments
questions.corrige_markdown:
Composition is the move from the parts to the whole: because each part has a property, we wrongly say the whole has it ("each brick is light, so the wall is light"). The reverse, from whole to parts, is the fallacy of division (C).

**Answer: A.**

choix.texte: One attributes the proprieties of the part to the whole.
The Conclusion is irrelevant to the premises.
One attributes the properties of the whole to the part.
The Conclusion doesn't follow from the premises.

questions.enonce_markdown: The study of Symbolic Logic is of great important because it:
themes: O Level Logic - symbolic logic basics
questions.corrige_markdown:
Symbolic logic replaces ordinary words by precise symbols, so it removes the ambiguity and vagueness of everyday language and makes the structure of an argument clear. It does not add obscurity (A), and special words and special reasoning are not the reason for its value.

**Answer: D.**

choix.texte: Involves the use of special words.

questions.enonce_markdown: Who amongst these logicians considered Logic and Mathematics as one?
themes: O Level Logic - nature and scope of logic
questions.corrige_markdown:
George Boole treated logic as an algebra, and Bertrand Russell (with Whitehead) argued that mathematics can be derived from logic. Together they stand for the view that logic and mathematics are one. Aristotle did not treat logic as mathematics, and Venn is known for his diagrams. Option A gives Whitehead without Russell, who is the leading figure of this thesis.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Identify the Proposition correctly punctuated below:

*Options as printed:* A) $(p \vee q) \cdot (r \cdot s)$   B) $(p \vee q \cdot r)$   C) $(p \vee q)(r \cdot s)$   D) $(p \vee q) \cdot r)$
themes: O Level Logic - symbolic logic basics
questions.corrige_markdown:
A proposition is correctly punctuated when every connective joins well-formed parts and the brackets balance. Option A, $(p \vee q) \cdot (r \cdot s)$, is well formed. Option B is ambiguous (no bracket tells whether the dot or the vee is the main connective), and C has no connective between its two groups. D, as printed, has an unbalanced bracket, but without that stray bracket it would be $(p \vee q) \cdot r$, which is also well formed. Because D can be read as a misprint of a correct form, two answers are defensible.

**Intended answer: A, $(p \vee q) \cdot (r \cdot s)$ (D only if its final bracket is a misprint).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically, so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following rules is applicable to Disjunction?
themes: truth tables and propositional logic
questions.corrige_markdown:
A disjunction $p \vee q$ is false only when both disjuncts are false: for $F, F$ the value is $F$. With $F,T$, $T,F$ or $T,T$ it is true (inclusive disjunction).

| $p$ | $q$ | $p \vee q$ |
|---|---|---|
| T | T | T |
| T | F | T |
| F | T | T |
| F | F | F |

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following symbolizes an Implication?
themes: O Level Logic - symbolic logic basics
questions.corrige_markdown:
The horseshoe $\supset$ stands for the conditional (implication) "if $p$ then $q$". The dot is conjunction, the vee is disjunction and the triple bar is equivalence.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: How many columns are required in constructing a Truth Table for the Function $(p \equiv q)$?
themes: truth tables and propositional logic

The table needs one column for each distinct variable and one for the function itself: a column for $p$, a column for $q$ and a column for $p \equiv q$, which makes three columns (and four rows).
